messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Leilani was nineteen when it happened, though she seldom speaks of that night in any form that holds together. She had been with him for almost a year, a man a few years older who she'd met through friends. He was charming at first, then possessive, then something else entirely. The evening that ended everything started over a disagreement about dinner—she couldn't remember the specifics, only the way his voice rose, the way he shoved her backward into the bedroom, and then the dark. He had flipped the light switch as he came after her, and the rest unfolded in blackness punctuated by sharp sounds: his palm against her cheek, the crack of her head against the wall, his breathing, her own choking sobs. When it was over, she lay on the floor for hours, too afraid to move, too afraid to turn the light back on and see her own face in the mirror.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani told herself she should have left earlier, should have known, should have spoken up before it got that far. She replayed the arguments, the warning signs she had ignored, and each time the guilt landed in her chest like a stone. When a close friend asked what happened, Leilani opened her mouth but the words scattered—she could not hold the sequence, could not make the beginning lead to the end, and eventually she just shook her head and stopped trying. Worse were the moments when the terror would wash over her without warning, without any image attached, as if her body remembered something her mind had misplaced. She would be sitting at her drafting table, focused on a client's color palette, and suddenly she was trembling, her heart hammering, and she had no idea why.

By the time she met her husband a year later, she had convinced herself that the past was over. She married quickly, wanting to feel safe, wanting to belong somewhere. But safety proved elusive. Her interior design work required her to meet clients in empty rooms, to walk through half-built spaces alone, and she found herself scheduling every appointment for midday when the light was fullest, when other people were nearby. She stopped taking evening consultations altogether. When male clients or contractors asked for a private walkthrough, she invented reasons for an assistant to come along, or she cancelled. One important client—a developer building a custom home—insisted on a late-afternoon meeting to review lighting options in the basement. Leilani could not explain why she refused; she simply said she was unavailable, and the client moved on. She lost the contract, but what frightened her most was not the lost income. It was the way her body had gone rigid the moment she imagined standing in that dark, unfinished room with a man she did not know.

She began to notice other patterns. She could not tolerate loud noises—a car backfiring on the street, a door slamming in the office—without her entire frame going tight, without scanning the room for an exit. She checked behind her constantly, even at home, even when her husband stood two feet away. She avoided being alone in any room with any man, including her own husband if the lights were dim or the door was closed. He did not understand why she flinched when he came up behind her, why she insisted on keeping every lamp on at night. She did not have the words to tell him, because when she tried, the story fell apart again—the thread lost, the guilt rising, the emotion outpacing any memory.

Now, at twenty, Leilani sits in a therapist's office for the first time. She came because she is exhausted, because her marriage is fraying, because she no longer recognizes the person she has become. She is certain her life has been destroyed, that she no longer belongs anywhere—not in her own home, not among friends, not even inside her own skin. She trusts no one, least of all herself. What she hopes for, though she can barely say it aloud, is that someone might help her find a way back to the light, and that she might one day walk into a room without first checking who is behind her.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Offender Cues: Seeing the offender: The vignette does not mention any encounter with the ex-partner or seeing the offender as a trigger.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

The glass shattered, but she did not hear it—she only felt her legs carry her out of the store, past the register, into the parking lot, where she crouched behind a car and shook until the manager came out to check on her. She never went back to that store. After that, she began scanning every crowd, every parking lot, certain he would appear again. She took longer routes home, avoided the neighborhood where he lived, and stopped going out after dark altogether.

She checked behind her constantly, even at home, even when her husband stood two feet away. She avoided being alone in any room with any man, including her own husband if the lights were dim or the door was closed. He did not understand why she flinched when he came up behind her, why she insisted on keeping every lamp on at night. She did not have the words to tell him, because when she tried, the story fell apart again—the thread lost, the guilt rising, the emotion outpacing any memory. Once, driving home from work, she thought she spotted him at a crosswalk—a man with the same build, the same stride—and she swerved into a side street, her heart hammering, and sat there for ten minutes before she could breathe normally again. She was certain she was being watched, that he was looking for her, that she would never be truly safe.

Now, at twenty, Leilani sits in a therapist's office for the first time. She came because she is exhausted, because her marriage is fraying, because she no longer recognizes the person she has become. She is certain her life has been destroyed, that she no longer belongs anywhere—not in her own home, not among friends, not even inside her own skin. She trusts no one, least of all herself. What she hopes for, though she can barely say it aloud, is that someone might help her find a way back to the light, and that she might one day walk into a room without first checking who is behind her, and that she might one day pass a stranger on the street without seeing his face.
